## Conclusion

Artificial intelligence is not defined by automation, speed, or the amount of data a system holds. It is defined by behaviour: a system perceives its environment, reasons about what it perceives, improves from experience, and chooses actions that serve a goal in situations nobody enumerated in advance. Ananya's rerouted ride showed all four in the space of a few seconds, which is why it counts as intelligent, whereas a timer that always runs for forty minutes does not.

Today's systems are intelligent in narrow, spectacular bands. That narrowness is not an accident or a temporary embarrassment; it is the direct result of the choices researchers made over seven decades, as the field swung from hand-written rules to systems that learn everything from data. Understanding why those swings happened, and what each approach got right and wrong, is what the evolution of AI paradigms explains next.

## Conclusion

The history of AI is not a smooth climb. It is a sequence of six answers to one question about where machine knowledge comes from, moving steadily from knowledge that humans write down to knowledge that machines extract for themselves. Each answer produced real successes, each hit a wall specific to its own assumptions, and each left behind techniques that are still running in production somewhere today.

That accumulated inheritance is why modern AI is not one thing. Logic and rules, probability, learned models, and generative systems all coexist, and a serious AI system today often combines several of them at once. Those coexisting specialities have names of their own, from natural language processing to computer vision to robotics, and mapping the branches of artificial intelligence is what the next lesson does.

## Conclusion

Artificial intelligence divides into branches because learning, perceiving, reasoning, and acting are genuinely different problems that reward different lifetimes of specialisation. Machine learning and deep learning study how knowledge is acquired, computer vision and natural language processing study how raw input becomes meaning, knowledge representation and expert systems and planning study how facts become decisions, and robotics studies how decisions survive contact with the physical world.

Two habits will serve you from here. Remember that the branches are nested and overlapping rather than parallel, so deep learning sits inside machine learning and appears inside almost every other branch. And remember the left turn: useful systems combine branches, so the interesting engineering questions usually live at the joins. What all of these branches share is that each is narrow, each solves one kind of problem well and nothing else, and that narrowness is precisely what the types of artificial intelligence classify next.

## Conclusion

Classifying AI by capability rather than technique gives three types, and the honest map is stark. Artificial Narrow Intelligence covers absolutely everything that exists, including systems that are superhuman inside their band, and its walls are built from three specific absences: no transfer between domains, no model of the world, and no goals of its own. Artificial General Intelligence remains an open problem with no agreed definition and a genuinely disputed timeline. Artificial Super Intelligence lies beyond that, hypothetical but not frivolous, since the alignment question it raises already applies to systems in production.

Carry one sentence out of this lesson: narrow does not mean weak, it means bounded, and the interesting question about any system is never how clever it seems but where exactly its boundary lies. Those boundaries are drawn very differently depending on whether a system was built from hand-written rules or learned from data, and that contrast between symbolic AI and learning-based AI is what the next lesson examines directly.

## Conclusion

Symbolic AI and learning-based AI are two answers to the question of where a machine's knowledge comes from, and each buys its strengths with a specific weakness. Rules give you transparency, predictability, and provable correctness, and they pay for it with brittleness and an inability to cope with anything their author did not foresee. Learning gives you flexibility, perception, and improvement from data, and it pays for it with opacity, unpredictability, and failures that arrive dressed as confident answers.

The mature position is not to prefer one. It is to look at a problem and ask which parts are messy perception, which parts are non-negotiable policy, and to use the right tool on each, which is exactly what hybrid systems do. With the paradigms, the branches, the types, and now the two great approaches in hand, the foundational vocabulary is complete, and the next lesson turns outward to see what all of it is actually being used for across healthcare, finance, agriculture, and the other domains where AI now earns its keep.

## Conclusion

AI applications look endlessly varied across healthcare, finance, retail, manufacturing, agriculture, transportation, education, and cybersecurity, but underneath they are five jobs repeated: predicting, perceiving, personalising, optimising, and generating. Naming the job cuts through most of the noise around any new product. Naming the four conditions for success cuts through most of the enthusiasm around any new proposal.

Sneha's father was wrong about AI being only for big companies, but he was right about something he did not say aloud: none of those four systems asked his permission, explained itself to him, or gave him any way to contest a decision it made about his customers. Every application in this lesson makes consequential decisions about real people, and asking who is accountable when those decisions are wrong or unfair is exactly what responsible AI takes up next.

## Conclusion

Responsible AI is not a layer of caution applied after a system works. It is a set of design decisions taken early, about which data is collected, which objective is optimised, which definition of fairness applies, whether individual decisions can be explained, who is accountable, and whether human oversight is genuine or ceremonial. Bias is not a flaw in the mathematics but an inheritance from data, proxies, and deployment, which is why deleting a sensitive column solves nothing and why Amazon's model discriminated without ever being shown a gender field.

The scale of these questions grows with the capability of the systems asking them, and capability is not standing still. Foundation models, multimodal systems, autonomous agents, AI in physical machines, and AI running on the device in your pocket are all arriving at once, each raising these same six questions in a sharper form, and where the field goes from here is what the final lesson of this unit examines.

## Conclusion

Five shifts are reshaping AI at once. Foundation models moved the expensive work of building capability away from individual teams, multimodal systems widened what a single model can take in, agentic systems turned outputs into actions, physical AI is attempting the same generalisation in machines that touch the world, and edge AI is moving all of it onto the device in your pocket. Each changes what is cheap and what is difficult, and each carries an unsolved problem worth knowing by name.

This closes the unit, so it is worth returning to the question it opened with: what makes a machine intelligent? Not automation, not speed, not scale. A machine earns the description when it perceives its situation, reasons about what it perceives, improves from experience, and chooses actions that serve a goal in circumstances nobody wrote down in advance. Everything since has refined that answer. Seven decades of paradigms shifted where the knowledge came from, the branches split the problem by what must be perceived and reasoned about, the types made clear that every system built so far is narrow however impressive it looks, symbolic and learning-based approaches offered two ways to install knowledge, applications showed what the whole apparatus is actually for, and responsible AI insisted that capability without accountability is not an achievement.

What remains is the mechanism. Knowing that an intelligent system perceives, reasons, and acts towards a goal is not the same as knowing how it does so, and the honest next question is the one that has driven the field since Dartmouth: given a goal, a situation, and a set of possible actions, how does a system actually work out what to do?

## Conclusion

An agent is anything that perceives through sensors and acts through actuators, and the whole of AI can be read as the study of how to choose those actions well. The vocabulary that makes this precise is small: percepts and percept sequences on the way in, actions and actuators on the way out, an agent function specifying the behaviour and an agent program implementing it. Rationality means selecting the action expected to maximise a performance measure on the evidence available, which is emphatically not the same as being right, being lucky, or knowing everything. And the performance measure must describe the state of the world you want, because an agent will optimise exactly what you wrote down.

Nandini's grandmother was not wrong that the vacuum behaved badly. She was wrong about the cause. The machine's limitation was in what it could perceive and retain, not in how it decided, and that is a distinction worth carrying into every system you meet.

Notice, though, that we have said nothing yet about what happens between the percept and the action. Two agents can receive identical percepts and behave completely differently depending on whether they keep a model of the world, pursue an explicit goal, or weigh competing outcomes against each other, and those internal designs are what agent architectures set out next.

## Conclusion

An agent architecture is what sits between percept and action. A simple reflex agent maps the current percept straight to an action and fails whenever history matters. A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using a transition model and a sensor model, which lets it operate when the sensors do not reveal everything. A goal-based agent reasons about the future towards an explicit target, gaining flexibility at the cost of computation. A utility-based agent scores outcomes on a scale, which is what allows it to handle competing objectives and uncertainty. And a learning agent wraps any of these in a performance element, learning element, critic, and problem generator, improving itself over time.

Rehana's five versions were not five ideas. They were one idea, repeatedly asked to remember a little more and consider a little further ahead, and the discipline worth taking from her is that each step up was forced by a specific failure rather than chosen for elegance.

There is something conspicuous about all five, though. Every one of them was designed against an assumption about what the rider's assistant is for, what it can sense, what it can change, and what counts as success, and none of those assumptions was ever written down. Setting them down precisely, before a line of code exists, is what the PEAS framework provides next.

## Conclusion

PEAS turns a vague intention into a specification. The performance measure states what success means as a property of the world, and must name every objective including the ones in tension, because anything left out has an implicit weight of zero. The environment draws the boundary of what the agent is accountable for. The actuators cap what it can ever achieve, and the sensors cap what it can ever know.

Vinay and Priyanka were not really arguing about a drone. They were arguing about a performance measure that no one had written, and an hour of that argument on day one, before any hardware was ordered, would have been the most valuable hour of the project.

Writing E as a list of things the agent will meet is only the beginning of understanding it, though. Two environments can contain exactly the same objects and still demand completely different algorithms, depending on whether the agent can see all of it at once, whether its actions have predictable results, and whether it changes while the agent is thinking. Those structural properties are what the classification of AI environments sets out next.

## Conclusion

Four structural properties decide what an agent is up against. Full observability means the current percept suffices, while partial observability forces the agent to maintain a belief about what it cannot see. Determinism allows a plan to be computed once and executed, while stochasticity forces continuous re-planning. A static environment grants unlimited thinking time, while a dynamic one imposes deadlines where a late answer is a wrong answer. And a discrete environment can be enumerated, while a continuous one must be discretised or handled with continuous mathematics.

Aditya's team learned the lesson the expensive way, which is that chess is not a simplified version of the real world but an unusually generous one, and an algorithm that assumed a friendly environment cannot simply be pointed at a hostile one.

For the rest of this unit, the environments will be deliberately friendly: fully observable, deterministic, static, and discrete. That is not a dodge. It is the only setting in which the core algorithms can be understood clearly, and every harder case is built on top of them. But even in that friendly setting, an algorithm cannot be pointed at a real problem directly. A corridor, a puzzle, or a delivery route has to be restated in terms of a starting situation, a set of available moves, a test for being finished, and a cost for each step, and turning a messy problem into those precise pieces is what problem formulation does next.

## Conclusion

Problem formulation is the bridge between a situation described in a sentence and an object an algorithm can accept. It requires five components: an initial state, the actions legally available from each state, a transition model saying what each action produces, a goal test, and a path cost naming what is being minimised. It also requires abstraction, keeping every detail that changes the available actions or the cost, and discarding everything else, with the check that any solution found must be one the agent can genuinely carry out.

The single most reliable source of error is an incomplete state. If you need the history to know which actions are legal, the state is missing something, which is why Ishaan's engineer must carry the set of sites already visited and the maze walker need carry only a pair of coordinates.

What all of this quietly assumes is that the collection of possible states, and the moves connecting them, form a structure that an algorithm can move around in. Making that structure explicit, seeing it as a graph of states joined by transitions, and understanding just how alarmingly large it becomes, is what state space representation takes up next.

## Conclusion

A state space turns a problem into a graph. States are complete descriptions of a situation, operators are the rules describing kinds of moves, transitions are specific applications joining one state to another, and a solution is a path from the initial state to any state satisfying the goal test. Nodes are the search's own bookkeeping and should not be confused with the states they carry.

Three facts about state spaces will shape everything that follows. They explode combinatorially, so enumeration is impossible for anything beyond a toy. Not all states are necessarily reachable, so a search can labour for hours over a question that a moment's arithmetic would show has no answer. And the representation you choose determines the size of the space, so merging genuinely identical situations into one state is often worth more than any algorithmic cleverness applied afterwards.

Sanjana's cousin's puzzle has 181,440 reachable arrangements, and somewhere among them is the one she wants. She cannot look at all of them. What she needs is a disciplined way to walk the graph, starting from where she is and expanding outward until the solved arrangement turns up, using nothing but the connections themselves. Strategies that do exactly this, with no hint about which direction the goal lies in, are the blind search algorithms taken up next.

## Conclusion

Blind search solves a real problem with almost no information. Given nothing but which places connect to which, breadth-first search fans outward ring by ring and returns a route through the fewest blocks, depth-first search commits to one corridor and trades that guarantee away for a much smaller memory footprint, and uniform cost search orders its frontier by accumulated cost and returns the genuinely cheapest route when the connections are not all equal. All three are the same algorithm wearing different frontiers: a queue, a stack, and a priority queue.

Farhan's exam is the reminder of why the third one mattered. The route through the fewest blocks took twenty-four minutes and the route through more blocks took sixteen, and an algorithm counting steps had no way to notice.

What none of the three can do is aim. Every one of them expands outward from the start with no sense of direction, which is tolerable on a campus of seven blocks and hopeless on a road network of millions, where a search that explores in every direction at once will exhaust a computer long before it reaches the destination. The obvious missing ingredient is some estimate, however rough, of how far each place still is from the goal, and using such an estimate to steer the search is exactly what heuristic search algorithms do next.

## Conclusion

A heuristic is an estimate of the remaining cost, and it converts search from a blind expansion into a directed one. Greedy best-first search orders the frontier by that estimate alone, which is fast and offers no guarantee at all, as the 35 km route through Lake View demonstrated. A\* orders the frontier by `f(n) = g(n) + h(n)`, combining the cost genuinely paid with the cost estimated to remain, and with an admissible heuristic it returns an optimal path while expanding far fewer states than uniform cost search.

The three algorithms are the same algorithm. Drop `h` and A\* becomes uniform cost search; drop `g` and it becomes greedy; inflate `h` and it slides back towards greedy, losing the guarantee on the way. Admissibility is what holds the guarantee in place, because an estimate that never overstates makes every `f` value a genuine lower bound, and a lower bound is what lets the search dismiss whole regions of the map without looking at them.

Every algorithm so far has been built to return a path, because the sequence of moves was the answer being sought. There is a large class of problems where that is simply not true. Asked to arrange a timetable with no clashes, nobody wants the sequence of edits that produced it; they want the timetable. When only the final configuration matters and the route to it is irrelevant, holding entire paths in memory is wasted effort, and the algorithms that exploit this are local search.

## Conclusion

Local search abandons the path and keeps only a current state, which makes it the natural tool for problems where the answer is a configuration rather than a route. It uses constant memory, tolerates state spaces far too large to enumerate, and can be stopped at any moment with a usable answer in hand.

Hill climbing moves to the best neighbour until none is better, which is fast and gets trapped by local optima, plateaus, and ridges, exactly as Latha's round stalled at 42.1 km against a possible 35.4. Random restarts escape by starting over, and reveal the shape of the landscape as a side effect, in this case four distinct peaks. Simulated annealing escapes without restarting, by accepting worse states with a probability that falls as the temperature drops, which explores early and settles late.

Underneath all three sits the same tension, and it is worth carrying beyond this lesson: exploiting the improvement in front of you and exploring in case something better lies elsewhere are in direct competition, and every one of these methods is a different answer to how much of each to do.

One assumption has held throughout every algorithm so far, including this one. The world has been indifferent. Roads do not rearrange themselves to lengthen your route, and stops do not move while the van is driving. Introduce a second party who chooses their own actions, who can see what you have done, and whose goal is precisely that you should fail, and every algorithm in this unit stops working, because the state that follows your move is no longer yours to determine. Searching under those conditions is adversarial search.

## Conclusion

Adversarial search handles the case where another party chooses alternate moves and wants you to lose. A game tree alternates MAX and MIN levels, and minimax passes values up by taking the maximum where the agent chooses and the minimum where the opponent does, which evaluates every move by its worst outcome under best opposition rather than its best outcome under lucky opposition. That is the discipline Manoj's first program lacked.

Minimax is correct and unusable beyond toy games, because game trees grow exponentially and chess and Go exceed any conceivable amount of computation. Alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that provably cannot change the answer, returning identical results for a fraction of the work, 18,297 positions against 549,946 on an empty tic-tac-toe board, with the saving depending heavily on examining good moves first. Beyond that, real engines stop at a fixed depth and substitute an evaluation function for the true value, which is the concession that made chess and Go programs possible at all.

Every problem in this unit so far, adversarial or not, has been about finding a *sequence*: a route through a campus, a tour of delivery stops, a line of play. Some problems are not sequences at all. Asked to fill a Sudoku grid or build a clash-free timetable, there is no journey to describe, only a set of variables that must each be given a value such that a list of rules is not broken. Problems of that shape have their own formulation and their own algorithms, and they are constraint satisfaction problems.

## Conclusion

A constraint satisfaction problem is defined by variables, domains, and constraints, and its solution is a complete assignment rather than a path. That difference is what makes the state transparent instead of a black box, and transparency is what lets a solver reason about which variable to tackle next rather than guessing.

Backtracking search is the core algorithm: assign provisionally, check the constraints, descend, and undo on failure. It works, and left to itself it wastes almost all of its effort, as the 4,208 placements for 51 blank cells showed. Choosing the most constrained variable first, the minimum remaining values heuristic, cut that to 51 with no backtracking whatsoever, because failing fast on the tightest variable is worth far more than making easy progress on loose ones. Degree, least constraining value, and constraint propagation extend the same instinct.

The reward for learning the formulation is reuse. Sudoku and Deepa's timetable share an algorithm and differ only in one function, which is what it means for a technique to be general.

That closes this unit, so it is worth answering the question it opened with. How do intelligent systems solve problems? By turning a situation into a precise formulation, representing the possibilities as a space of states, and then searching that space with a strategy suited to what is known. Blindly when nothing indicates the direction of the goal. With a heuristic when something does. Keeping only the current state when the path is irrelevant. Assuming the worst reply when an opponent is choosing alternate moves. And reasoning over variables and constraints when the answer is a configuration rather than a journey.

Every one of these techniques shares an assumption that is easy to miss because it was never stated. In all of them, the knowledge the agent needed was already sitting in the structure of the problem: the corridors on the map, the coordinates of the towns, the rules of the game, the list of clashes. Somebody handed that structure to the algorithm. Real intelligence has to hold knowledge about the world in a form it can reason over, work out consequences that nobody wrote down, and cope with facts that are uncertain rather than given, and that is a different problem entirely.
