## Conclusion

A knowledge-based system splits what a system knows from how it reasons. The knowledge base holds domain facts and rules, the inference engine applies them while knowing nothing about the domain, working memory holds the case in hand, and the explanation facility can say which rules were used. That split is what allows knowledge to be inspected by the expert who owns it, corrected without touching the program, reused across domains, and defended to whoever is affected by the decision.

MYCIN showed both halves of the story: roughly six hundred rules performing comparably to specialists at diagnosing blood infections, and a system that never treated a patient because adequacy is not the same as deployment. The industry that followed collapsed on the difficulty of extracting knowledge from experts, and the architecture itself is still running today wherever a decision has to be explainable, in loan eligibility, prescription checking, and configuration validation.

Ramesh's manager filled eleven pages and captured almost nothing, and it is worth being precise about why. The problem was not that Ramesh knows too much. It is that "write down what you know" is not a well-defined instruction until somebody decides what a written-down piece of knowledge actually looks like: whether it is a fact, a rule, a procedure, or a definition, and what form each of those takes so that a machine can use it. Deciding that is knowledge representation, and it is what the next lesson takes up.

## Conclusion

Knowledge representation is the decision about what a piece of knowledge looks like once written down. Facts record what is true now, and are inert on their own. Declarative knowledge states what is true, which makes it reusable across purposes, readable by the expert who owns it, and safe to change in one place. Procedural knowledge specifies how to do something, which is faster and captures skill that resists being stated, at the cost of being opaque and single-purpose. The two are not different kinds of knowledge but different encodings of it, and choosing between them is an engineering decision that should follow what is likely to change and how many purposes the knowledge must serve.

Any scheme is judged on whether it can express the domain, support derivation, do so efficiently, and be populated at reasonable cost, and those four pull against each other so consistently that practical systems deliberately choose the least expressive scheme that will do the job. Beyond that sit the two questions a representation can never avoid: what silence means, and what stays unchanged when something changes.

Anjali's problem was never that she lacked knowledge about her father's mornings. It was that her system offered her timers and triggers, and none of what she knew would fit in either. Give her a way to write "if he is likely to bathe soon then start the geyser" and the system can finally hold the thing she has known all along. Rules of exactly that shape, and the machinery that fires them, are what rule-based reasoning provides next.

## Conclusion

A production system holds facts in working memory and general knowledge in a rule base, and drives them with a recognise-act cycle that matches rules against facts, resolves which eligible rule to fire, and adds the conclusion so that further rules become applicable. Iqbal's diagnosis, which looked like instinct, turned out to be four such steps in sequence, and the trace the engine produces is an explanation the customer can be shown.

When several rules are eligible at once, conflict resolution decides which fires, using rule order, specificity, recency, or explicit priority. In a rule base that only adds facts, this changes the path but not the destination, and that comfortable property disappears as soon as rules are allowed to retract facts. One rule base serves every case, including combinations nobody traced by hand, and it is honest enough to conclude nothing when the facts are insufficient.

What the engine has been doing throughout deserves closer inspection. It concluded "spark problem suspected" from "fuel or spark problem" together with "tank has petrol", and that step is only valid because of something about the structure of the statements themselves, entirely independent of scooters. Whether a conclusion genuinely follows from what is known is not a question about mechanics, and answering it precisely requires a formal language for statements and the operations that combine them. That language is propositional logic.

## Conclusion

Propositional logic gives statements a fixed meaning. Each proposition is definitely true or false, five operators combine them, and each operator is defined completely by its truth table, so a formula's meaning does not depend on how anyone reads it aloud. Because a formula over n propositions has 2 to the power n possible situations, every one can be enumerated, which turns questions that are arguments in English into checks that a machine performs exhaustively.

That enumeration is what classifies a formula as a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency, and what decides whether two formulas are equivalent. It is also what caught Tanvi's missing brackets in six of sixteen situations, including a disarmed flat with an open door at three in the morning. Watch for inclusive OR, and watch for implication, whose vacuous truth is a convention and whose converse and inverse are both invalid while its contrapositive is sound.

The ceiling arrives early, though. Tanvi can specify one flat precisely and has no way to say "any armed flat in the building", because propositional logic has no notion of a flat as a thing that properties can hold of, and no way to state that something is true of all members of a collection or of at least one. Adding objects, the properties and relations that hold of them, and the ability to quantify over them, is what first-order predicate logic does next.

## Conclusion

First-order predicate logic breaks statements open. Objects are the things in the domain, predicates are properties that hold of them, relations connect several at once, and functions map objects to other objects. That structure alone lets a system see that two statements about two students are instances of one pattern, which propositional logic could never do.

Quantifiers do the rest. The universal quantifier states something about every object and pairs with implication; the existential states something about at least one and pairs with conjunction; and getting that pairing backwards produces statements that are either absurdly strong or vacuously true. Negation swaps one quantifier for the other, and when quantifiers of different kinds are nested, their order changes the meaning, which is the difference between every student having an advisor and one exhausted person advising every student.

Farida's 4,200 propositions collapse into a handful of statements that survive next year's intake. The price is real: exhaustive checking is gone, inference is only semi-decidable so a system may never return an answer of no, and quantification is restricted to objects rather than properties.

Both this lesson and the last built languages for *stating* what is known, and stopped there. Neither said what it means for one statement to genuinely follow from others, nor how a machine could establish that it does. Tanvi's alarm table and Farida's rulebook are both inert until something can take what is written and derive what was not. Defining that relationship precisely, and computing it, is logical inference.

## Conclusion

Logical inference rests on entailment, and entailment is defined over situations rather than procedures: a statement is entailed when it is true in every model in which the knowledge base is true. Model checking computes this directly by enumerating models, discarding those the knowledge base rules out, and testing what remains. It is the clearest way to see what the definition means, it hands you a counterexample when entailment fails, and it becomes impossible as soon as the number of propositions grows.

Deduction manipulates the statements instead, which scales, and it must therefore be judged against entailment. A sound procedure derives only what is genuinely entailed, and this is not negotiable. A complete procedure can derive everything entailed, which is desirable but survivable in its absence, since an incomplete sound procedure merely fails to answer rather than answering wrongly. Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid for any statements whatsoever; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are not, and both fail in the same situation, which is the one Nikhil walked into with a router under his arm.

Both programs in this lesson computed entailment by grinding through every model, and both would collapse at thirty propositions. Real systems do not work that way. They start from what they know and push forward to whatever follows, or they start from the question and work backwards to what would have to be true, and those two directions of travel behave very differently in cost, in what they compute, and in which questions they suit. Choosing between them is what inference techniques covers next.

## Conclusion

Forward and backward chaining apply the same rules in opposite directions. Forward chaining is data-driven: it starts from what is known, fires every applicable rule, and derives everything derivable, which on the office network meant eight rules fired and five facts nobody asked for. Backward chaining is goal-driven: it starts from the question, finds rules that would establish it, and recursively pursues their conditions, which meant three rules examined and a trace that doubles as a proof.

The difference that decides real deployments is not the rule count but the question count. Backward chaining asked a technician five questions where forward chaining would have needed ten observations gathered in advance, which is exactly why consultation systems reason backwards and monitoring systems reason forwards. Neither is faster in general, since relevance depends entirely on which goal is being pursued, and forward chaining wins outright when many questions must be answered against one set of facts.

Everything in this unit so far has represented knowledge as isolated statements: facts, rules, propositions, predicates. That works, and it hides something. When a system knows that a laser printer is a printer, that a printer is a network device, and that network devices have IP addresses, those three facts are not independent. They form a structure, and the structure itself carries knowledge, because the system should be able to work out that a laser printer has an IP address without anyone stating it. Representations built to make that structure explicit are semantic networks, frames, and ontologies.

## Conclusion

Semantic knowledge models make structure explicit so that the arrangement of knowledge does inferential work. A semantic network joins entities with labelled arrows and supports inheritance along is-a links, which lets a system answer questions no stored fact addresses and keeps the knowledge base small. Frames group everything about a concept into slots, adding typical values as defaults and allowing procedures to be attached, which reconciles declarative and procedural knowledge in one representation. Ontologies formalise the vocabulary itself, with classes, typed properties, cardinality constraints, and axioms, which makes consistency checkable and lets separate systems mean the same thing by the same word. Knowledge graphs take the uniform triple to industrial scale and produce the panels you see beside search results.

Two cautions travel with all of them. Distinguish is-a from instance-of, since one relates categories and the other places an individual in a category. And accept that inheritance with exceptions makes the reasoning non-monotonic, so a new fact can withdraw an earlier conclusion, which is a real departure from the logic of the previous lessons and the price of representing a world where birds usually fly.

Notice, though, what every representation in this unit has quietly assumed. Facts have been true or false, rules have fired or not, and inheritance has delivered a definite answer. A doctor examining a patient with a fever has none of that. The fever is consistent with several conditions, some far more likely than others, the tests are informative rather than conclusive, and treatment cannot wait for certainty. No amount of structure fixes this, because the difficulty is not that the knowledge is badly organised but that it is genuinely uncertain, and representing degrees of belief rather than truth values is where the unit turns next.

## Conclusion

Reasoning under uncertainty replaces true and false with a degree of belief between 0 and 1, and Bayes' theorem is the rule for revising that belief when evidence arrives. The posterior combines the likelihood, meaning how well the hypothesis predicts the evidence, with the prior, meaning how plausible the hypothesis was beforehand, normalised by how likely the evidence was overall.

The prior is the term people drop, and dropping it produced the entire misunderstanding at the screening camp. A test that catches 99 of every 100 ill people, applied to a population where only 1 in 100 is ill, generates 495 false alarms against 99 true ones, so a positive result means one chance in six rather than ninety-nine in a hundred. The same test yields anything from 0.2 percent to 95 percent depending only on the population it is used in, which is why evidence has no fixed strength of its own and why screening programmes are targeted. Counting whole people out of 10,000 rather than juggling decimals makes all of this far harder to get wrong.

Every calculation here involved one hypothesis and one piece of evidence. Real diagnosis does not look like that. A physician weighs several possible conditions against a fever, a cough, a travel history, a blood count, and an age, where the conditions compete with one another and the symptoms are not independent, since one condition causing a fever changes how informative a second symptom is. Writing out the full table of probabilities for even ten such variables requires over a thousand numbers, and for thirty variables the table is larger than any hospital could ever fill. Representing which variables actually depend on which, so that the whole picture can be assembled from a handful of small tables, is what Bayesian networks do.

## Conclusion

A Bayesian network solves the problem that a full joint distribution is both unfillable and dishonest. By recording only direct influences as arrows in a directed acyclic graph, and giving each node a small table of probabilities conditional on its parents alone, it reconstructs the whole picture from a handful of numbers that an expert can actually supply. The saving grows with the model, because the full table doubles with every variable while each node's table depends only on its parents.

The idea underneath is conditional independence: once a variable's parents are known, the rest of the network tells it nothing more. Reasoning then flows in both directions, causally from causes to effects and diagnostically from effects back to causes, and the network reproduces explaining away without being taught it, so that confirming one cause of an observed effect properly reduces belief in an alternative. Note the asymmetry that makes the graph more than a picture: observing a common cause removes a dependence between its effects, while observing a common effect creates one between its causes.

Everything in this unit has now been about knowing. Rules, logic, entailment, structure, and probability have all served the question of what a system believes about the world, and what follows from it. Believing is not acting. A warehouse robot that knows a parcel is on shelf four, that its gripper is empty, and that the packing bench is at the far end has not thereby moved anything. Turning what is known into an ordered sequence of actions that transforms the current situation into a desired one is a different task, and it is what AI planning takes up next.

## Conclusion

AI planning turns knowledge into action. A state is a set of facts, a goal is a partial set of facts that must hold, and each action is described by its preconditions, its add list, and its delete list, with everything not mentioned left unchanged. That last convention is what makes the representation practical, since it dissolves the need to say what an action does not affect.

Because actions are described rather than programmed, a planner can find sequences nobody anticipated, and the constraints emerge from the descriptions themselves: the robot came back for the second parcel because the gripper precondition made it impossible to do otherwise. The cost is exponential in plan length, which is why states explored went from 8 to 52 to 410 for one, two, and three parcels, and why real planners derive heuristics automatically from the action descriptions rather than searching blindly.

That closes this unit, so it is worth answering the question it opened with. How do intelligent systems represent knowledge and reason? By separating what is known from how it is used, so knowledge can be inspected and corrected. By choosing a form for that knowledge, declarative or procedural, and accepting what each choice costs. By writing rules and firing them, in whichever direction the question demands. By using logic when statements are definitely true or false, and probability when they are not. By making structure explicit so that categories carry properties down to their instances. And by turning all of it into an ordered sequence of actions when something actually has to be done.

Every technique in this unit shares one requirement, though, and it is the thing to carry forward. Somebody had to supply the knowledge. Iqbal's fault patterns, Tanvi's alarm conditions, the prevalence of a disease, the arrows in a Bayesian network, the preconditions of picking up a parcel: each was written down by a person who already understood the domain. The systems reasoned impeccably over knowledge they were given and could not acquire a single fact for themselves. What happens when nobody can write the knowledge down, and the system has to extract it from examples instead, is a different discipline entirely.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/01_int:
## Conclusion

Machine learning inverts ordinary programming. Instead of supplying rules and data to obtain answers, you supply data and answers to obtain rules, in the form of a model whose adjustable numbers are fitted to the examples. That inversion is worth making in one specific circumstance: the pattern is real, nobody can state it, and examples exist in quantity. Devika's threshold rules needed no learning; the senior accountant's sense of what a vendor's invoices normally look like could never have been written down.

A claim to be doing machine learning is only meaningful if you can name a task, a performance measure that is genuinely a number, and the experience the system learns from. Training fits the model, and inference applies it, and the two are separated in practice because one is expensive and rare while the other is cheap and constant. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning are nested rather than parallel, so a route planner is AI without learning and a decision tree is learning without any neural network.

The costs are equally real. Learning requires labelled data, inherits every bias in how that data was collected, offers accuracy rather than guarantees, and can be difficult to explain to the person its decision affects.

Devika's problem happens to come with the answers attached, since every invoice in her database is now known to have been fine or fraudulent. That is one situation among several. A system might instead be given data with no answers at all and asked to find structure in it, or be given no data up front and left to discover what works by trying things and observing the results. Those are fundamentally different learning situations requiring different methods, and sorting them out is what the learning paradigms do next.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/02_lea:
## Conclusion

The learning paradigms are distinguished by feedback, not by subject matter. Supervised learning has a correct answer attached to every example and aims to predict that answer for new ones, splitting into classification for categories and regression for continuous quantities, with labels rather than data as the binding constraint. Unsupervised learning has no answers and aims to find structure, through clustering, dimensionality reduction, or anomaly detection, and carries the permanent difficulty that without an answer key there is no clean way to establish that a result is correct. Reinforcement learning receives rewards after actions rather than answers about examples, and faces two problems the others do not: feedback that arrives long after the decisions that caused it, and a dataset the agent generates through its own choices.

The Jaipur team's error was assuming three requests were one job. Asking what tells the system it was right, for a single example, separates them immediately, and the honest answers were "the eventual repayment", "nothing", and "the time the trip took".

Two paradigms in this unit remain a matter of naming rather than doing, and one does not. Reinforcement learning is a subject in its own right and is introduced here as a paradigm rather than developed. The supervised and unsupervised methods, though, are what the rest of this unit builds, and every one of them begins from the same place: a table of examples with columns that have to be chosen, rows that have to be split, and quantities that have to be measured before any algorithm can touch them. Getting that table right is what data for machine learning covers next.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/03_dat:
## Conclusion

A dataset is a table where rows are examples, feature columns are what the model may see, and the label column is what it learns to predict. Features come as numeric, categorical, ordinal, or binary, and the categorical ones need encoding that does not invent an order that is not there. The features chosen set a ceiling on achievable performance, and no algorithm gets past a ceiling imposed by columns nobody collected.

The rows are split before training so that the model can be measured on data it has never seen, with the shuffle applied before the cut and the seed fixed for reproducibility. On a small dataset a single split is itself unreliable, as the 68.2 against 55.3 lakh averages showed.

Above all, every feature must survive one question: will this value be known at the moment the prediction has to be made? Harsh's model was near perfect because it was predicting the price from the price, and data leakage of that kind is discovered in production rather than in development, which is what makes it the most expensive mistake in this lesson.

The table is now in a usable shape, with features separated from a label and rows divided into training and test. Nothing has yet been learned from it. The first and most direct thing to attempt is to find a relationship between the features and a label that is a continuous quantity, so that an unseen flat of 1,100 square feet can be given a price in lakh rather than a category. That is regression.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/04_reg:
## Conclusion

Regression predicts a continuous quantity. A straight-line model has one slope per feature and an intercept, and least squares chooses them by minimising the sum of squared vertical distances between the data and the line, which for a single feature can be computed directly with no search. Applied to twelve flats it produced roughly 7.6 lakh per hundred square feet and estimated an unseen 1,100 square foot flat at 74.1 lakh.

Error is summarised by mean absolute error, which is the average miss in the label's own units, and root mean squared error, which punishes large misses more heavily. Neither means anything without a baseline, and the honest baseline is to ignore every feature and always guess the training mean. Beating it by a wide margin is the minimum evidence that a model has learned something.

Two cautions matter more than the arithmetic. The slope is interpretable and the intercept usually is not, since it describes a flat of zero area. And a test error lower than the training error, as happened here at 0.52 against 3.57, is a signal that the test set is too small to measure anything rather than evidence of an unusually good model.

Regression works because the label is a number on a scale, where being off by two lakh is meaningfully better than being off by twenty. A great many important questions are not like that. Whether an invoice is fraudulent, whether an email is spam, whether a patient has a condition: these have no scale, no in-between, and no meaningful notion of being slightly wrong. Predicting a category rather than a quantity requires a different kind of model and a completely different way of measuring success, and that is classification.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/05_cla:
## Conclusion

Classification predicts a category rather than a quantity, so being slightly wrong is not a meaningful idea and the model's job is to carve the feature space into regions rather than fit a line through it. Binary problems have two categories and multi-class problems have three or more, and for some methods that difference is trivial while for others it requires real extra machinery.

k-nearest neighbours classifies by resemblance: find the most similar labelled examples and take a vote. It needs no training, extends from two categories to three without modification, and made sensible decisions on Rohini's messages where two hundred banned phrases had failed in both directions. Its single setting, k, controls how much the prediction is smoothed, with small values sensitive to noise and large values collapsing towards always predicting the most common category, as the accuracy of exactly zero at k equal to 13 showed. Its costs are real: no summary of the data, sensitivity to feature scale, no explanation a person can act on, and degradation as features multiply.

The explanation problem is the one to carry forward. Rohini's classifier works and can only justify itself by pointing at other messages. A bank, an examinations board, or a hospital needs a decision that can be stated as a rule, read by the person it affects, and challenged if it is wrong. A model that produces exactly that, a readable chain of yes-or-no questions ending in a verdict, is the decision tree.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/06_dec:
## Conclusion

A decision tree splits the data one feature at a time, choosing at each node the feature and threshold that most reduce impurity, and continuing until the groups are pure or a limit stops it. Gini impurity measures how mixed a group is, and the split that lowers the weighted average impurity most is the one taken. Thresholds are discovered from the data rather than supplied, and the search is greedy, so the tree produced is good rather than optimal.

The result is the only model in this unit whose prediction and explanation are the same object. The Belagavi bank's tree fits on a sheet of paper, tells a rejected applicant exactly which threshold they missed, and converts directly into a numbered list of rules that a compliance officer can check against policy.

The weaknesses are equally definite. Trees keep splitting until leaves describe individuals, which is why the depth-2 tree contained a rule resting on one applicant. They are unstable under small changes to the data. And the ensembles that fix the accuracy problem destroy the readability that motivated the choice in the first place.

Every model so far in this unit has needed labels. Rohini's classifier needed messages already sorted into folders, and this tree needed sixteen applications whose outcomes were known. Now suppose the bank wants to understand its customers rather than score them, and asks what kinds of customer it has. Nobody has ever labelled a customer as belonging to a type, and no amount of waiting will produce such labels, because the types are not recorded anywhere. Finding structure in data that carries no answers at all is clustering.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/07_clu:
## Conclusion

Clustering finds groups in unlabelled data using resemblance alone. k-means picks k centroids, assigns every point to the nearest, moves each centroid to the average of its members, and repeats until the assignments settle. Applied to the chain's customers it recovered four genuinely different kinds of shopper, each of which the marketing head can address differently.

It only did so after scaling. On the raw numbers, annual spend ranged over tens of thousands while visits ranged over twenty, so distance was determined by spend alone and two entirely different customer types were merged into one group. For any method that measures distance, deciding how features are scaled is part of the model rather than a preparatory chore.

Two properties need permanent scepticism. k-means converges to a local optimum that depends on where it started, as the fifth seed's inertia of 0.592 against the others' 0.098 demonstrated, which is why it is run repeatedly and the best result kept. And because clustering has no answer key, the number of groups is chosen by reading an elbow rather than computed, the algorithm returns tidy groups even from structureless data, and the meaning of any group is supplied by a person rather than discovered by the method.

Across this unit, several choices have now been made with no principled basis. The value of k in the nearest-neighbour classifier was picked by eye. The maximum depth of the loan tree was set to three. The number of clusters here was set to four and then justified after the fact. Each of these is a setting chosen before learning begins rather than learned from the data, and getting them wrong quietly wastes most of a model's potential. How such settings are chosen honestly, and how a model is trained so that the choice can be trusted, is what model training addresses next.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/08_mod:
## Conclusion

Training a model is arithmetic. Making its measured performance mean something is a discipline, and this lesson is about the second.

A single train-test split reports one draw from a distribution. On twelve flats, two hundred shuffles of the same model and the same data produced scores from 0.52 to 5.74 lakh, so Sameer's excellent result and Ritu's poor one were the best and worst of the same thing. k-fold cross-validation trains k times, holding out each part once, and reports an average with a spread, which on this data gave 3.01 lakh give or take 1.67. The spread matters as much as the average, because it says how much to trust the estimate.

Parameters are learned from data and hyperparameters are chosen before training, which means they must be chosen by measuring, which requires held-out data of its own. Hence three sets: training to fit, validation to choose, and test opened exactly once at the end. Tuning on the test set produced a reported error of 3.75 lakh against an honest 7.44, and picked a worse value of k while doing it.

Every measurement in this lesson has been mean absolute error, a single number summarising how far predictions fall from the truth. For a price in lakh, that is a reasonable summary. For a classifier it is not, and the reason matters: the mail system whose 98 percent accuracy comes from labelling everything junk, and the loan model that is right about most applicants while being wrong about every applicant of one particular kind, are both excellent by a single-number measure and both unusable. Choosing measurements that reveal such failures rather than hiding them is what model evaluation takes up next.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/09_mod:
## Conclusion

A single accuracy figure can be high while a model is useless, and on rare-class problems it usually is. Ninety-eight percent accuracy was achieved by a model that found nobody, and it outscored a model that found four cases in five.

The confusion matrix holds the actual information in four counts: cases found, cases missed, false alarms, and correct clearances. Recall is the fraction of real cases caught, precision is the fraction of flagged cases that were real, and F1 combines them into one number at the cost of hiding which is weak. Each is defined with respect to one chosen class, and each can be driven to a perfect score by a degenerate model, which is why they are quoted in pairs and read alongside the counts.

Most classifiers produce a score rather than a decision, and the threshold that turns one into the other trades recall against precision continuously. That threshold is a policy choice belonging to whoever bears the cost of each kind of error, and a model shipped with it fixed has quietly made someone else's decision for them.

Every measurement in this lesson was taken on data the model had not trained on, which is what made it meaningful. That raises the question this unit has circled several times without confronting directly. A model can be made to score perfectly on the data it learned from, simply by being flexible enough to memorise it, and such a model is usually the worst one to deploy. Understanding why more flexibility eventually makes a model worse, and how to recognise the point where that begins, is model generalization.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/10_mod:
## Conclusion

Generalization is performance on data the model has not seen, and it is the only performance that matters. A model underfits when it is too rigid to represent the pattern, scoring poorly on training and test alike, and overfits when it is flexible enough to absorb the noise, scoring superbly on training and badly on new data. The diagnosis comes from the gap between the two scores rather than from either alone.

Increasing flexibility always reduces training error, all the way to exactly zero at degree 9, which is why training error is never evidence that a model is good. Test error follows a different shape entirely, falling to a minimum and then rising, and the model with zero training error was the worst on the table at 1.281. Inspecting predictions between the training points showed why: the overfitted curve was not slightly wrong but wildly unconstrained, answering minus 3.22 where the truth was 0.34.

Two remedies work, and they address different situations. Reducing flexibility helps when the model is chasing noise. Adding data helps for the same problem without changing the model, taking the degree 9 fit from 1.352 to 0.187 while its training error rose from 0.000 to 0.219. Neither helps underfitting, which needs a more capable model or better features.

Every algorithm in this unit has been written out by hand, in plain Python, so that nothing was hidden: least squares, nearest neighbours, impurity and splitting, centroids and reassignment, cross-validation, and the metrics. That was deliberate, and it is not how the work is done in practice. A handful of well-tested libraries implement all of it, correctly and efficiently, in a consistent interface that makes swapping one model for another a one-line change. Seeing the same work done that way, and understanding exactly which parts you no longer have to write, is what machine learning with scikit-learn covers next.
4 - Machine Learning Fundamentals/11_mac:
## Conclusion

scikit-learn gives every model the same interface: `fit` to learn, `predict` to apply, and constructor arguments for anything you choose yourself, with learned values stored under names ending in an underscore. That uniformity is the library's real contribution, because it makes comparing four models a loop rather than a project.

The tools matching this unit's lessons are all there. `train_test_split` with `stratify` splits fairly, `cross_val_score` replaces hand-written folds and returns the spread as well as the mean, `make_pipeline` binds preparation to the model so that scaling is refitted inside each fold rather than leaking across them, `DummyClassifier` supplies the baseline every result must beat, and `GridSearchCV` tunes hyperparameters inside the training data so the test set stays closed until the end.

What it does not supply is the judgment. It computed a coefficient saying flats further from the city centre cost more, and reported it without complaint, because noticing that a number is nonsense is not something a library can do. Deciding whether the problem needs learning, which features are honest, which metric matters, and where the threshold belongs are all still yours.

That closes this unit, so it is worth answering the question it opened with. How do intelligent systems learn from data? By inverting the usual relationship, taking examples and their answers and deriving the rule rather than receiving it. By choosing a model whose shape suits the problem: a line for a quantity, a boundary for a category, a readable tree where the decision must be defended, centroids where nobody has labelled anything. By measuring on data the model has never seen, with quantities chosen to expose the failure that matters rather than to flatter. And by resisting the pull towards flexibility, since the model that fits its training data perfectly is reliably the worst one to deploy.

Every model in this unit worked on a table of numbers that a person had already decided upon. Somebody chose that area, bedrooms, age, and distance were the columns worth having; somebody reduced an email to a count of links and exclamation marks. That choice set a ceiling on everything that followed, and for tables it is a ceiling humans can usually reach. For a photograph, a recording, or a paragraph of text, nobody can say which numbers to extract, and the whole approach stalls. Systems that learn the features themselves, directly from raw input, work on a different principle entirely.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/01:
## Conclusion

A biological neuron receives signals through dendrites, sums excitatory and inhibitory contributions in its cell body, and fires down its axon when the total crosses a threshold, with synapses setting how strongly each connection counts and changing that strength with experience. Three features of this were borrowed: many simple units, weighted connections that adapt, and a threshold producing the output. Timing, chemistry, growing new connections, learning from a couple of examples, and learning without a supplied answer were all left behind.

The comparison with a computer is most useful where it fails. Neurons are millions of times slower than transistors and there are tens of billions of them working simultaneously, which is why the lesson to take is about parallel architecture rather than speed. Memory and processing being the same thing in the brain, and separate in a computer, is a difference that still constrains hardware today.

The name invites three misunderstandings worth resisting: that these networks work as brains do, that larger means more brain-like, and that neuroscience is a reliable guide to better systems. Engineering diverged from biology decades ago and follows whatever works.

What survived is a single claim of real power. A unit that computes a weighted sum and applies a threshold is doing nothing intelligent, and a great many of them, connected by numbers found from data rather than chosen by a designer, can do a great deal. Making that concrete means building the unit itself, seeing exactly what a weighted sum and a threshold can decide, and that is the artificial neuron.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/02:
## Conclusion

An artificial neuron has four parts: inputs arriving as numbers, one weight per input saying how much and in which direction it counts, a bias setting how much total evidence is demanded, and an activation function turning the accumulated total into an output. Positive weights push towards firing and negative weights push against, which is how the word "unless" in a plain-English brief becomes a number.

The unit's structure never changes. One six-line function produced a working irrigation controller, an AND gate, an OR gate, a NAND gate, and a rule that ignores one of its inputs entirely, purely by being handed different numbers. That separation, fixed structure and behaviour held in the numbers, is what makes learning possible at all, because numbers can be nudged in response to a mistake while a structure cannot. A weight of zero is the neuron's way of saying an input is irrelevant, and the bias is its threshold, taking the same weights from always-on through OR and AND to never firing.

Two limitations were left hanging deliberately. The numbers in this lesson were all chosen by hand from a brief somebody had already written out, which is precisely the situation machine learning exists to avoid. And the exercise asked you to build a neuron that fires when exactly one of two inputs is active, which cannot be done, for a reason that is not obvious yet.

Both threads lead to the same place. A procedure that finds the weights from labelled examples, rather than requiring a person to work them out, is what turns this unit into a model that can learn. That procedure, and the precise geometric reason for the failure you just met, is the perceptron.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/03:
## Conclusion

The perceptron adds a learning rule to the artificial neuron, so the weights come from examples instead of from a person. The rule updates only on mistakes, moves each weight in the direction that would have corrected the error, and touches only the connections whose inputs were active. Starting from all zeros it rediscovered the AND gate in six epochs, and on real student records it found a boundary trading study hours against attendance that nobody had written down.

What it learns is always one straight line. That is enough for a great many problems and it is a hard ceiling. The convergence theorem promises a solution in finite time whenever a separating line exists, and says nothing at all when one does not, in which case the rule cycles indefinitely while looking exactly like slow progress. XOR is the smallest example: two points needing one label sit on opposite corners of a square, and no line can separate them from the other diagonal.

Notice what the failure is not. It is not a shortage of data, a badly chosen learning rate, or insufficient training. It is the shape of the model. One neuron draws one line, and the problem needs something a line cannot express.

The exercise above pointed at the way out. OR is a line. NAND is a line. XOR is what you get by combining them, which means the answer is not a better line but a second stage of processing that works on the outputs of the first. Stacking neurons into layers so that later ones operate on what earlier ones computed is the feedforward neural network.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/04:
## Conclusion

A feedforward network arranges neurons in layers, each receiving the previous layer's outputs, with information flowing one way and no loops. That single change removes the perceptron's ceiling. Three neurons, each still drawing one straight line, computed XOR correctly on all four cases, because the hidden layer moved the points into a space where a straight line was enough.

That is what hidden layers do. They do not draw curves; they re-describe the input so the next layer's straight line suffices. Forward propagation is the repetitive application of one operation, weighted sums followed by an activation, with a two-layer network and a two-hundred-layer network running the same three lines a different number of times. Since the network is nothing but a nested list of numbers, learning means changing that list.

The activation function turned out not to be a detail. Removing it from the XOR network produced an output of −0.5 for every possible input, and the algebra shows why: a weighted sum of weighted sums is a weighted sum, so any depth of purely linear layers collapses into one layer and every added layer is wasted.

That result raises the obvious question. The activation used here was a hard threshold in one program and a smooth curve called sigmoid in another, with no explanation of the difference. It matters more than the choice of any weight, because the wrong activation can make a deep network untrainable no matter how good everything else is, and the shift to one particular activation is a large part of why deep learning began working when it did. Those choices are what activation functions covers next.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/05:
## Conclusion

The activation function is what keeps layers from collapsing, and its shape decides whether a deep network can be trained at all. Sigmoid maps into 0 to 1 and tanh into −1 to 1, both following a smooth S that flattens at both ends, while ReLU passes positive inputs through unchanged and zeroes the rest.

Flatness is the problem. Training asks how much a weight matters, and the answer is proportional to the steepness of the activation at that point, so a saturated neuron sitting far from centre has stopped learning while still producing output. Sigmoid's steepest possible slope is 0.25, reached only at its midpoint.

That ceiling compounds with depth. A correction passing back through ten sigmoid layers is multiplied by at most 0.25 ten times, arriving at under one millionth of its size, and at fifty layers the figure has thirty zeros after the decimal point. The early layers of a deep sigmoid network receive nothing. ReLU's slope of exactly 1 for active neurons removes the compounding entirely, which is a large part of why deep networks became trainable. Its cost is that neurons stuck on the negative side receive no correction and die, which leaky ReLU mitigates.

Choose ReLU for hidden layers by default, and choose the output activation separately according to what the answer needs to look like.

Throughout this lesson the phrase "the correction travelling back through the layers" has done a great deal of work without ever being explained. Something computes how wrong the network is, works out which direction each of thousands of weights should move, and applies those changes repeatedly until the network is right. That process, from measuring the error to distributing the blame across every layer, is what training neural networks covers next.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/06:
## Conclusion

Training turns a network of random numbers into one that works, using three ideas. A loss function converts being wrong into a single number, producing a landscape whose height is the error and whose position is the weights. Gradient descent measures the slope of that landscape and steps downhill, automatically taking large steps when far from the bottom and small ones when close, with the learning rate scaling every step. Backpropagation makes the slope computable in a multi-layer network by passing blame backwards, each neuron's share being the error of what it fed multiplied by the connecting weight and by its own responsiveness.

Put together, they trained a 2-2-1 network to compute XOR from four examples and random starting weights, reaching a loss of 0.00013. The nine numbers that had to be reasoned out by hand two lessons ago were found by the network itself, and nothing in the code knew what XOR was.

The failure modes are as important as the procedure. A saturated activation makes the gradient vanish before it reaches the early layers. A learning rate that is too large diverges and one that is too small never arrives. And the loss landscape of a real network has many hollows, so where the random weights start decides which one is found, which is why the same code succeeds on one seed and stalls on another.

Everything so far has worked on inputs somebody chose: three sensor readings, two binary values, one distance in kilometres. The reason to build networks at all is that for photographs, recordings, and text, nobody can say which numbers to extract. A network deep enough to construct its own useful inputs from raw data, layer by layer, is doing something categorically different from fitting a model to features a person supplied, and that difference is what deep learning means.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/07:
## Conclusion

Deep learning removes the feature engineering stage. Where the older pipeline required a person to convert raw input into a few hundred meaningful numbers, a deep network takes the raw input directly and produces its own intermediate descriptions in the layers between input and output.

Those descriptions turn out to be hierarchical: edges, then corners and textures, then repeated motifs, then object parts, then whole objects. The first layers rediscover detectors that vision researchers had designed by hand, which suggests the network is finding something real, and the later layers reach abstractions nobody built successfully. Each layer describes the input in terms of what the previous layer found, so capability comes from composition rather than from any layer being clever.

Depth beats width because composition is efficient, features get reused, and the parameter count stays smaller. And it began working around 2012 not because the ideas were new but because large labelled datasets, graphics processors, ReLU, and a handful of practical techniques arrived together.

The costs are real. Deep networks want far more data and compute, and their learned features are unnamed, so explaining a decision is genuinely hard. They are the right tool for raw perceptual input and frequently the wrong tool for a table of twenty columns, where simpler models match them while remaining fast and explainable.

One difficulty was skipped over. A fully connected layer treats every pixel as unrelated to every other, so a photograph shifted a single pixel presents an almost entirely different input, and connecting a modest image to a first hidden layer already costs a hundred thousand weights before the network has learned anything. Both problems have the same cause, which is that the architecture knows nothing about images being arranged in space. Building that knowledge into the structure itself is what convolutional neural networks do.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/08:
## Conclusion

A convolutional network builds the structure of images into the architecture. A small filter of learned weights is slid across every position, multiplying and summing the pixels it overlaps, and the resulting feature map records how strongly that filter's pattern matched everywhere. The operation is local, uses the same weights at every position, and preserves the grid layout so that convolutions can be stacked.

Pooling then keeps the strongest response in each small block, cutting the data by three quarters in the example here, widening what later layers effectively see, and deliberately discarding precise position so that small shifts stop mattering.

Together these fix both failures of a fully connected layer on images. Ten parameters replaced 1,332 for a single feature on a tiny image, with the gap widening sharply as images grow, and the same filter detected the same bar with identical strength in every position it was placed. That is weight sharing and translation invariance, and they are why a network can recognise something in a corner of a photograph having only ever seen it in the centre.

Stacked into a real network, convolution and pooling alternate while the spatial size shrinks and the number of feature maps grows, producing the edges-to-textures-to-parts-to-objects hierarchy, with fully connected layers at the end turning parts into a verdict.

All of this rests on one assumption: that the input has a fixed size and a spatial layout where neighbours are related. A photograph satisfies it. A sentence does not. Words arrive one after another, the important relationship is order rather than adjacency in a grid, and there is no fixed length, since a review may be eight words or eight hundred. Handling input that arrives as a sequence, where what came earlier changes the meaning of what comes now, requires a network with something convolution does not have, which is memory.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/09:
## Conclusion

A recurrent network reads a sequence one element at a time, updating a hidden state from the current input and the previous state, using the same weights at every step. That state is the only memory, and it lets order matter: three pairs of sentences containing identical words gave identical bag-of-words scores and clearly different recurrent readings.

The memory is also the weakness. Each step multiplies the carried state by the recurrent weight, so influence from early words decays exponentially, reaching about one percent after twenty steps at a weight of 0.8. Pushing the weight above 1 to preserve information makes the state grow without limit instead. There is no value that both remembers far back and stays stable, which is the long-range dependency problem, and LSTMs addressed it with explicit gates and a channel along which information can travel largely undisturbed.

A second limitation proved just as consequential. Because each step depends on the one before, the computation cannot be parallelised, so recurrent networks could not exploit the hardware that made everything else in deep learning fast.

Both problems come from the same design decision: forcing all information about the past through one state, passed hand to hand along the sequence. If a word nineteen positions back matters, it has to survive nineteen handovers to be heard.

The alternative is to stop passing information along a chain and let every position look directly at every other position, deciding for itself which ones are relevant. Distance stops mattering, since everything is one step away, and every position can be computed at the same time. That mechanism is attention.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/10:
## Conclusion

Attention replaces the chain of handovers with direct access. A query is compared against every key, the comparisons become weights summing to 1, and the result is the correspondingly weighted blend of the values. The blending is what makes it trainable, since smooth weights give gradient descent something to work with, where a hard selection would not.

In self-attention every position produces a query, key, and value, so each word's new representation is a mixture of all words weighted by relevance to it. Two consequences follow, and they are exactly the two problems recurrence could not solve. Any position reaches any other in a single step, with no decay however far apart they are, and every position can be computed simultaneously rather than in order.

The price is that attention has no notion of sequence at all. Shuffling the words left every attention weight unchanged, because a score compares two vectors and nothing in that comparison mentions where either sat. Order has to be reinstated deliberately, by adding a positional vector to each word before attention runs. The other price is quadratic cost, since every pair is compared, which is why long contexts are expensive.

Attention is a mechanism rather than a complete architecture. It says how one position gathers information from others, and says nothing about how many such layers to stack, what to do between them, how to build an encoder that reads and a decoder that writes, or how to train the whole thing at scale. Assembling attention into a full architecture, and the design that did it, is the transformer.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/11:
## Conclusion

A transformer is a stack of identical blocks, each containing multi-head self-attention, a position-wise feedforward network, and residual connections with normalisation around both. Multiple heads let a position track several kinds of relevance at once, with heads specialising without being told to. Residual connections give the training correction a path that skips layers, which is what makes depths of dozens of blocks trainable, and normalisation keeps the numbers stable as they flow through.

The original design paired an encoder, which sees the whole input in both directions, with a decoder, which generates one token at a time while masked from seeing ahead and using cross-attention to consult the encoder. The three modern families correspond to keeping the encoder, the decoder, or both, and the decoder-only family turned out to be unexpectedly general.

It displaced recurrence because training parallelises completely, because distance between positions costs nothing, and because it scales predictably enough to justify very large investments. It pays for this in quadratic attention cost with sequence length.

What the architecture does not supply is any notion of truth, any memory beyond its context window, or any resemblance to how brains work.

There is one more thing the architecture alone does not explain. A transformer is a shape, and a shape does nothing until it has been trained. The systems that write code, answer questions, and translate were not built separately for those tasks; one very large model was trained once on an enormous quantity of text and then adapted, cheaply, to all of them. That change in how models are built and reused is what foundation models describes, and it closes this unit.
5 - Neural Networks and Deep Learning/12:
## Conclusion

A foundation model is trained once, on an enormous quantity of unlabelled data, using a self-supervised objective where the label is already present in the data. Predicting a hidden word requires no annotation, so the supply of training examples is limited only by how much text exists, and the capability that emerges from pursuing that simple objective at scale is a by-product rather than something directly taught.

That expensive pre-training then serves many purposes. Full fine-tuning, partial fine-tuning, few-shot prompting, and zero-shot prompting form a ladder of adaptation methods needing progressively less data and less compute, with the bottom two requiring no weight changes at all. It works because earlier layers learn general structure that almost any related task needs, so adaptation is only learning the specific part.

The costs are not technical. Capability concentrates in the few organisations able to pre-train, their choices propagate into everything built downstream, a flaw in one model can appear in thousands of applications, and a model that does an unbounded set of tasks cannot be exhaustively evaluated. And the models remain fluent without being accurate, fixed at a knowledge cut-off, and resistant to having new facts installed by fine-tuning.

That closes this unit, so it is worth answering the question it opened with. How do modern AI systems learn complex representations? By stacking simple units, each computing a weighted sum and an activation, into layers where each layer re-describes what the previous one found. By training those layers with gradient descent and backpropagation, which required activation functions that do not flatten and connections that let corrections skip layers. By building the structure of the data into the architecture, with convolution for images and attention for sequences. And by doing the expensive general learning once, on enough data that the representations transfer to problems the model was never built for.

The through-line is worth stating once more. A neuron cannot separate two classes on a diagonal. Everything in this unit was built out of that neuron.
