## Conclusion

Natural language processing covers three distinct activities: turning characters into structured units, extracting meaning, and generating language. The first is mechanical and consequential, since every step of tokenising, lowercasing, removing stopwords, and stemming discards something, and deleting negations from a stopword list is a common way to build a sentiment system that reports the opposite of the truth.

TF-IDF finds what makes a document distinctive by weighing each word against how rare it is across the collection, giving words that appear everywhere a weight of exactly zero. It needs no stopword list because commonness penalises itself, it takes twenty lines, and it is still a reasonable baseline for search and classification.

Its weakness is that it treats a document as an unordered bag. Counting single words scored "the food was not good" as positive; counting pairs fixed that and could not reach a negation separated from its target by an intervening clause. No fixed window can, which is why the field eventually abandoned fixed windows.

Four difficulties define the domain: ambiguity needing outside knowledge, dependencies at arbitrary distance, unbounded variation in how people write, and complaints that contain no complaint word and are understood only by knowing how the world works.

Language is one kind of raw input a person can interpret instantly and a machine cannot. It is not the only one. A photograph presents the same problem in a different form: a grid of brightness values that means nothing until something turns it into objects, boundaries, and categories, and the systems that do that are computer vision.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/02_co:
## Conclusion

Computer vision extracts meaning from images, and its difficulty is that a picture arrives as a grid of numbers in which nothing marks an object, the same object produces wildly different values under different conditions, different objects can produce similar values, and the dimensions are enormous.

The field divides into tasks of increasing demand: classification assigns one label to an image, detection locates objects with boxes, semantic segmentation labels every pixel by category, and instance segmentation separates individual objects. The labelling cost rises steeply along that sequence and is usually what decides which a project can afford, so the right choice is the least demanding task that answers the actual question.

Deployed systems illustrate different concerns. Face unlock succeeds partly because verifying one enrolled face is far easier than recognising anyone, and it runs on the device by design. Medical imaging is a rare-class problem where accuracy is meaningless and the threshold is a clinical judgment, which is why the systems assist rather than decide. Autonomous driving needs several tasks at once, in real time, in conditions nobody controlled.

The failures are systematic. Models degrade under distribution shift, latch onto spurious correlations such as a hospital's marker rather than the disease, can be flipped by imperceptible changes to an image, and perform unevenly across demographic groups when training data under-represented them. All of these follow from the same fact: a model learns what distinguishes its training examples, which is not always the subject a person had in mind.

Images are one raw signal that means nothing until something interprets it. Sound is another, and it adds a difficulty images do not have, since a photograph sits still while speech arrives over time, must be segmented into words nobody separated, and carries an accent, a pace, and a room's echo on top of the words themselves.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/03_sp:
## Conclusion

Speech AI turns audio into text and text into audio, and it sits in front of any language system that people talk to. It differs from text processing in ways that matter: speech has no spaces between words, the same word is never produced identically twice, the signal is enormous and mostly redundant, it arrives over time without the option of re-reading, and noise is mixed inseparably into the same signal as the voice.

Recognition converts the waveform into a frequency representation, maps that onto units of sound, and uses a language model to choose the plausible word sequence, with modern systems training the whole chain end to end rather than building the stages separately. The transport line's failures were all recognisable: rare place names the language model had not seen, mixed-language speech it was never trained on, noise absent from its clean training audio, and older speakers missing from the data. The standard remedy for the third is deliberately degrading the training recordings, which is a general technique worth knowing.

Word error rate is the usual measure, it can exceed 100 percent, it weights a missed article the same as a missed destination, and a figure quoted without saying what audio it was measured on tells you very little.

Synthesis has a different set of difficulties: deciding how written text should be pronounced, producing prosody that carries meaning, and reaching a naturalness that now makes voice imitation a practical fraud mechanism.

The applications so far in this unit have interpreted something a person gave the system: a review, a photograph, a spoken request. A different class of system is not interpreting anything you provided. It watches what a great many people did and predicts what you will want next, without being told anything about you directly, and that is recommendation.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/04_re:
## Conclusion

A recommendation system chooses a small number of items from a catalogue too large to browse. Content-based filtering describes items by their attributes, builds a profile from what a person liked, and scores everything against it, which works from the first rating and can explain itself, at the cost of over-specialisation: a profile of action thrillers recommends action thrillers forever.

Collaborative filtering ignores the items and uses other people, predicting a rating from what similar viewers thought. It knew nothing about Office Hours, not its genre, cast, or plot, and predicted a rating of 3.22 purely from the pattern of who liked what. That is why it often outperforms attribute-based methods and why its suggestions can surprise usefully.

It fails structurally on cold start. A new title has no ratings, and a new subscriber resembles nobody, both returning nothing at exactly the moments that matter most commercially. Content-based methods cover both gaps, which is why real systems are hybrids.

Beyond the mechanics, what a recommender is told to maximise determines what it does. Clicks reward misleading presentation, watch time optimises for time spent rather than time well spent, and predicted rating narrows towards the familiar, while the thing actually worth maximising takes months to observe. Feedback loops and popularity bias then entrench whatever the system already favours, which is why deliberate exploration is built in.

The systems in this unit so far all sit at a distance from the world: they read text, look at pictures, listen to audio, or rank a catalogue, and if they are wrong, something is mislabelled or badly suggested. A machine that moves has no such buffer. It must perceive, decide, and act continuously in a physical space where being wrong breaks something, and that is robotics and autonomous systems.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/05_ro:
## Conclusion

Robotics differs from every other application in this unit because it acts on the physical world. Errors cannot be undone, deadlines are real, commands do not translate reliably into motion, and the environment changes while the machine is deciding. Perception is a component of the problem rather than the problem.

The loop has four stages. Perception fuses several sensors because none is reliable alone. Localisation determines where the machine is, drifting steadily when relying on wheel rotations and correcting against recognised landmarks, which is why covering the floor markers disabled a robot that could still see perfectly well. Planning chooses a route and must be redone constantly as the map changes. Control converts the plan into commands and corrects the gap between what was commanded and what happened.

SLAM resolves the circularity of needing a map to localise and a position to map, building both together, with loop closure correcting accumulated error when a place is recognised as already visited.

Autonomy is a spectrum from teleoperation to full independence, and the level requiring a human to remain alert for hours and intervene within seconds is the one that fails for reasons of human attention rather than engineering. Learning is used more sparingly here than elsewhere because data collection is slow, exploration is expensive, and behaviour learned in simulation does not transfer cleanly to real hardware.

Every system in this unit so far has taken something in and produced a judgment about it: a label, a transcript, a ranking, a movement. A different class of system does not judge anything. Given a prompt it produces an essay, an image, or a working function that did not previously exist, and the shift from recognising to producing changes what these systems are for and what can go wrong with them.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/06_ge:
## Conclusion

Generative AI produces artefacts rather than judgments, and that is a larger task than classification, because a classifier may ignore everything not needed to separate categories while a generator must supply the whole. The mechanism across families is the same in spirit: learn the structure of a large body of examples, then sample from it. Text models predict the next token repeatedly; image models learn to reverse a noising process one small step at a time and generate by running that reversal from pure noise, guided by a description.

The practical variable is how cheaply the output can be checked. Code can be run, images can be glanced at, and factual text may take longer to verify than to write, which explains why adoption ran fastest in programming and design rather than tracking output quality.

The publishing house's gain was not replaced judgment but collapsed cost per candidate, which moves the bottleneck from producing to specifying and selecting. That makes these tools strongest for exploratory work where a person selects and refines, and weakest where the first output must be right and nobody is placed to check it.

Four problems are structural: fluency without accuracy and no signal about which parts to doubt, training data taken from people who were not asked, occasional close reproduction of that data, and a collapse in the cost of producing convincing false material. A fifth is subtler, which is that heavy use converges everyone on the same average style.

Of the four output types, one has become far more consequential than the others, because text is not only an output format but the interface through which people now instruct these systems, ask questions of them, and connect them to other software. Understanding what a model built purely on predicting the next token can and cannot do, and what determines the quality of what comes back, requires looking specifically at large language models.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/07_la:
## Conclusion

A large language model predicts the next token, and three properties of that arrangement explain most of what practitioners run into.

Tokens are subword pieces from a fixed vocabulary, so cost tracks tokens rather than words, unusual names and other scripts fragment into many pieces and cost several times more for identical meaning, and the model does not see letters at all, which is why it is poor at counting characters or spelling backwards.

The context window is everything the model can see, and it holds no memory beyond it. The support assistant contradicted itself because at turn 25 the earliest exchanges had been dropped to make room, and nearly half the window was consumed by instructions and pasted policy before the customer typed anything. Continuity is manufactured by the surrounding software, not by the model.

Sampling explains the inconsistency. The model's scores are the same every time; temperature decides how faithfully they are followed, from near-deterministic at 0.2 to a 6.2 percent chance of a token the model rated poorly at 3.0. A factual assistant belongs near zero, and shipping one at a creative setting is an avoidable error.

Adaptation runs from clear instructions, through worked examples, to retrieval, to fine-tuning, and the cheapest sufficient method is the right one. Retrieval is what most projects actually need, since it supplies facts the model cannot know, allows citation, and updates by editing a document. Fine-tuning teaches form more reliably than it teaches facts.

All of this concerns text alone. The systems now being deployed accept a photograph of a damaged parcel alongside the complaint about it, read a chart and discuss what it shows, or watch a video and answer questions about what happened. Handling several kinds of input within one model raises a question none of this unit has yet addressed, which is how an image and a sentence can be made comparable at all.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/08_mu:
## Conclusion

Multimodal systems accept more than one kind of input, and the problem they solve is that a sentence and a photograph have nothing in common as data. The answer is to map both into a shared vector space where related things land near each other, trained on the enormous supply of images that already come with text attached, using a self-supervised objective that requires no manual labelling.

Once both modalities occupy the same space, comparison becomes distance, search across modalities becomes a nearest-neighbour lookup, and a language model can accept image vectors alongside token vectors. It also yields zero-shot classification, where categories are supplied as phrases at the time of asking rather than fixed during training, which is why a new damage category costs a sentence rather than a labelled dataset.

The capabilities run from cross-modal search and captioning through visual question answering to joint reasoning, and the last is the one that changes the work: checking a description against evidence was not previously automatable, and it is exactly what caught the claim describing severe damage over photographs of a scratch.

Grounding helps and does not cure. A model answering about an image in front of it invents less, and it can still misread the image and describe the misreading fluently, and the output does not distinguish a correct reading with false reasoning from a misreading with sound reasoning.

This unit has now covered systems that read, look, listen, rank, move, and generate. Every one of them does a single thing when called and stops. The insurer's assessor does not stop: they read the claim, decide a valuation is needed, look one up, notice a discrepancy, request another photograph, and only then reach a judgment. A system that chooses its own sequence of steps, calls other software along the way, and continues until a goal is met is doing something none of these do, and that is an AI agent.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/09_ai:
## Conclusion

An AI agent places a model in a loop with tools, memory, and a stopping condition, so that instead of answering once it works towards a goal across several steps. The model never executes anything; it requests a tool call and surrounding software decides whether to honour it, which means everything the agent can do is defined by the program rather than the model. Tools also cover for what models do badly, which is why an agent is given a calculator rather than asked to multiply.

The limit on agents is arithmetic. Reliability multiplies across steps, so a component working nineteen times in twenty produces a twenty-step task that succeeds barely a third of the time, and this explains most of the distance between a five-step demonstration and a twenty-step deployment. Retrying closes much of the gap, taking an eight-step task from 43.8 percent to 92.7 with a single retry, but only for steps that can safely be repeated. Sorting tools into repeatable and not is the most consequential design decision in building one, and it is ordinary software engineering.

Beyond that sit permissions, spend caps, loop detection, logging, and the treatment of anything a tool returns as data rather than as instructions.

An agent that acts on the world raises a question sharply that a model answering a question raises only softly. When the expense agent rejects a claim, the claimant will ask why, and "the weighted total was above zero" is not an answer anybody can act on or appeal. Producing a reason a person can check, challenge, and act on is a separate problem from producing a correct decision, and it is what explainable AI addresses.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/10_ex:
## Conclusion

Explainable AI produces an account of a decision that the person responsible for it or affected by it can check, challenge, and act on. It matters because a system nobody can interrogate is a system professionals override or ignore, which is what ended the Kochi trial despite the model being accurate.

There are two routes. Build a transparent model, where the explanation is the model itself, or build the best performer and reconstruct an explanation afterwards, accepting that the reconstruction is an approximation. The trade between accuracy and explainability is genuine in some cases and assumed in many more: here a readable rule matched the opaque model exactly, so the transparency cost nothing and was given away by default.

Permutation importance explains from the outside by scrambling one column and measuring the damage, which works on any model however opaque and correctly identified that the marker carried almost everything. It reports importance across a whole dataset rather than for one case, and it understates features that duplicate each other.

Counterfactual explanations answer the question people actually ask, which is what would have had to be different. They only help when restricted to things that can change, and deciding which features those are is a human judgment the model cannot make.

Different audiences need different forms: the person affected needs actionable advice, the professional needs a basis for trusting this case, the maintaining team needs to know whether the model is right for the right reason, and a regulator needs documentation. An explanation that sounds convincing without being faithful raises trust without raising trustworthiness, which is the worst outcome available.

Explanation addresses a system behaving as designed and being hard to understand. A different set of problems arises when a system does not behave as designed: when a small deliberate change to an input flips a confident decision, when instructions arrive hidden inside data the system was asked to process, or when a model optimises exactly what it was told to and produces something nobody wanted. Those failures are the subject of AI safety and security.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/11_ai:
## Conclusion

AI safety and security concerns failures under adversarial pressure and failures of objective, and both differ from ordinary error because average performance stops being the relevant measure.

Adversarial examples exploit the gap between a model's boundary and the concept it approximates. Two words removed from a spam message moved it across the filter's boundary while leaving it obviously spam to any reader, and the attacker needed no access to the weights, only the ability to observe outcomes and try again. Adversarial training, rate limits, and model ensembles raise the cost without removing the problem.

Prompt injection is structurally worse because there is no separation between instructions and data. Printing the two prompts side by side shows the operator's rules and a stranger's instructions arriving in one flat block with equal authority, and the secret sitting in the prompt where the model can see it. Filtering fails: a phrase list caught two attempts out of six, defeated by extra spaces, by rewording, by hiding the request in another task, and by simply asking. Input filtering enumerates an infinite set; the defences that hold restrict what the system may do, not what the input may say.

Alignment failures involve no adversary. The system pursues its stated objective faithfully, and the objective was a proxy that came apart under optimisation, which is the performance-measure problem from the start of this course reappearing with more capable systems attached.

All three are reasons that building a model is a small part of shipping one. A system that works on a test set may be defeated by an adversary, may be uninterpretable to the people meant to rely on it, and may optimise something nobody intended, and none of that appears in an accuracy figure. What a project actually has to do, from stating the problem through to monitoring a deployed system, is the AI development lifecycle.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/12_ai:
## Conclusion

The lifecycle runs from problem definition through data, model development, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring, and the effort is distributed almost the inverse of expectations. Model development is the stage least likely to kill a project, and it is where nearly all the attention goes.

Problem definition has to establish what decision changes, who is accountable when the system is wrong, and what threshold counts as good enough, all agreed before any results exist. Data is usually the longest stage, and the checks that matter are whether each feature will be available at prediction time, whether the data comes from the period the model will face, who is represented, and how the labels were produced. That last carries a specific trap, since outcomes are observed only for cases that were approved, so the training data omits precisely the population the model most needs to judge.

Deployment is a workflow problem rather than a modelling one, deciding where the prediction appears, what form it takes, what the person may do with it, and what happens when it is unavailable. Shadow deployment and staged rollout are ordinary practice and frequently skipped on the mistaken grounds that testing on historical data is the same as testing in service.

Monitoring separates a system from a project. Performance decays through data drift, concept drift, and pipeline breakage, and the third is the most common and produces no error message, because a model given nonsense returns confident nonsense. Watch the input distributions, the prediction distribution, outcomes as they arrive, and above all the human override rate, since the people closest to the decisions notice before the metrics do.

The bank's model was accurate and lasted eleven months. Nothing that killed it would have appeared in an accuracy figure.

This course opened by asking what makes a machine intelligent, and has spent six units answering it: perceiving, representing, reasoning, learning, and acting. What remains is the direction of travel, since the systems described here are not a settled state of the art but a snapshot of a field moving quickly, and the last lesson looks at where it appears to be going and how to judge such claims.
6 - Modern Artificial Intelligence/13_em:
## Conclusion

Five directions describe where effort is currently going. Agentic systems that act rather than answer, held back by reliability compounding across steps. Physical AI bringing recent capability to machines that move, held back by the cost of real-world data and the gap between simulation and hardware. Edge AI running models on devices for reasons of latency, privacy, cost, and connectivity, held back by model size. AI for science searching spaces too large to explore by hand, held back by verification that has not accelerated. And efficiency rather than scale, pursued partly because the supply of good training text is finite.

Only one of the five is about raw capability. The rest concern deploying capability that already exists into settings that resist it, which is a reasonable description of where this field currently is.

Several things have not improved and have repeatedly been described as nearly solved: learning from few examples, reliable factuality, robustness to adversarial input, causal understanding, and faithful explanation of a specific decision.

Six questions will serve you better than any forecast. What exactly was demonstrated and on what, is it a task or a job, what is the failure rate and what happens on failure, what else has to be true, who benefits from your belief, and what would change your mind.

This course opened at a junction in Bengaluru, with an app that rerouted a rider around a lorry it had never been told about, and asked what made that intelligent. The answer took six units: it perceived, it represented what it perceived, it reasoned about what followed, it had learned from data nobody hand-coded, and it acted towards a goal. Every system since has been a variation on those four capabilities, assembled differently and at different scales.

What you should take from it is not the current state of any technique, which will date. It is the ability to look at a system, name which of the four it is doing, ask what it was trained on and what it is optimising, work out how it will fail, and decide whether it should be built at all. That was the skill worth acquiring, and it does not expire.
